title: 1.5.23 Spot the Broken Pseudocode
description: Five multiple-choice questions on reading a broken plan, indentation, and why nothing running it is the point. Checked instantly.

questions.question: Read the plan above literally, one line at a time. What makes the loop never finish?
options: count starts at 1 instead of 0
The loop is missing a closing brace
print cannot be used inside a loop
Nothing ever changes count, so "count is less than 10" stays true forever
questions.explanation: The condition tests count, and no line touches count. It is true on the first pass and true on every pass after.

questions.question: Which change fixes it?
options: Add "add 1 to count" at the end, not indented
Change "less than 10" to "less than 100"
Add "add 1 to count" indented inside the loop, under print count
Move "set count to 1" inside the loop
questions.explanation: It has to be inside the loop, or it runs once after the loop is already stuck. Indentation is what puts it inside.

questions.question: What is indentation doing in pseudocode?
options: Making the plan look tidy for the reader
Showing which steps are inside which: it is containment, not decoration
Marking which lines are the most important
Standing in for the semicolons that pseudocode does not use
questions.explanation: Move one line in or out by four spaces and you have described a different program. That is how much work it is doing.

questions.question: Nothing checks pseudocode: there is no compiler for it. Why is that an advantage rather than a problem?
options: A syntax error tells you nothing about whether the plan makes sense, so a human reading it is the check that matters
It means you can write the plan as carelessly as you like
It makes pseudocode faster for the computer to run
It means mistakes in pseudocode cannot happen
questions.explanation: The bug here is a planning bug. No compiler would have caught it; reading it aloud catches it in seconds.

questions.question: This plan was caught by reading it, not by running it. Why would running it have been the worse way to find this particular bug?
options: It would refuse to start, giving no information at all
It would produce the right answer and hide the problem
It would take too long to type in
It would print forever without ever pointing at the line responsible
questions.explanation: An endless stream of numbers tells you something is wrong and nothing about what. The plan tells you exactly what.
